title: Five Underrated Tequila Cocktails
summary: Go beyond the Margarita, from the Negroni-like Rosita to the tropical Toreador.
content:
In the tequila canon, the immense popularity of the Margarita and Paloma (and their many riffs) has left some other classics overlooked. From spirit-forward drinks to tropical classics and even an unexpected agave-based aperitif, the world of tequila drinks beyond these headliners is vast, and worth exploring. Here are five underrated recipes to start with.

Guadalajara Punch is a regional favorite in Jalisco, Mexico. The large format drink combines various citrus fruits with soda, tequila and salt. It’s served in a clay vessel and is sometimes called the Cazuela Voladora, or “flying casserole”; its easy-drinking nature can “send you flying.” (See also: Cantarito, another tequila classic served in earthenware.)

title: Rolo’s Wine Program Is On Fire
summary: After a fire ravaged its cellar, the restaurant made a quick pivot—to the delight of wine lovers.
content:
In early August, Leo Bayless-Hall woke up to a nightmare. He’d gotten up early to open the weekend brunch shift at Rolo’s, the popular Ridgewood, Queens restaurant where he’s beverage director, only to receive the news that a refrigerator in the basement had caught fire in the middle of the night. Luckily, the street-level dining room and the apartments above were left unscathed. But tragically, the fire claimed the Rolo’s wine room, eviscerating almost every bottle in their extensive, carefully curated beverage program. “I went in before cleanup had started,” Bayless-Hall recalls. “It looked like the whole place—the walls, the doors, the fridges, the shelves, the bottles, everything—was coated in a jet black layer of smoke.” 

Many of the bottles had exploded; others were covered in the melted wax from their caps. Some laid entirely empty, their corks making a break for it in the heat of the flames. The fire remediation team wiped down every remaining bottle and placed them back on their shelves, allowing Bayless-Hall and the rest of the Rolo’s team to investigate the extent of the damage. Quickly, it became clear that none of the wine from their basement storage was salvageable. “We knew right away that we weren’t going to be able to sell these bottles of wine,” Bayless-Hall explains. Upon examination, some of the collection was fine, “but a few of the bottles were really gross, and had clearly been maderized, or cooked.” Rolo’s made the devastating decision to ditch their entire list, rather than risk a bad pour: “If every single bottle is going to be a dice roll, we have to just take it all as an L.” 

It was a tough call for Bayless-Hall in particular. Since he took over as beverage director two years ago, he has doubled the wine list at Rolo’s, focusing on adding American wines, especially from the East Coast, to the menu, as well as diversifying the offerings within broad categories like Riesling and Burgundy. “I had a real attachment to some of this stuff,” he says.

But in a lucky twist of fate, Bayless-Hall’s rapacious hunt for new bottles provided a life raft for Rolo’s after the fire. The collection had become so vast that they acquired an offsite storage location at the beginning of the year. It wasn’t meant to be a contingency for emergencies: “I’d been buying some cooler, older stuff,” he explains. “They were well above the standard price point for what we had been offering. We were slowly figuring out ways to put some of that stuff onto the menu, but a lot of it was waiting in the wings.” After the fire, the Rolo’s team decided to open up their offsite collection as a way to keep serving great wine while they rebuild what they lost. 

By the following weekend, Rolo’s was ready to start offering these pours, with the aim of keeping the price relatively stable from their old list, despite the higher costs of the bottles. “Every wine director will always brag about how good their prices are,” Bayless-Hall says. “But now that we got forced into this position, it’s important to us that people keep thinking about Rolo’s as a place to drink wine that is well-priced and accessible. That means that, for the time being, our markups are the lowest they’ve ever been.” He estimates that the current markup is, on average, a third or even half the restaurant’s typical pricing. For more premium bottles, he adds, they’re selling them almost at cost: “I just want us to break even.” 

So far, he says, the backup plan seems to be a success. Whether it’s because the staff is thinking more about wine than they would otherwise, or because the prices are better than they might have been before the fire, Bayless-Hall has noticed an uptick. “It’s only been a few days, but we’re selling more wine.” 

Since the fire, the team has been opening one special bottle a night, offering pours of rare wines like a 2002 Robert Ampeau & Fils Les Charmes Mersault (“super lactic and intense,” according to Bayless-Hall), a jeroboam of a 2025 Peter Lauer “Kupp No. 8” Riesling Kabinett (with “really tightly wound acidity” and “zesty citrus”) and a 2013 Thomas Perseval Le Village Blanc de Blanc (“low-intervention, zero sulphur added, and zero dosage with 7 years on the lees is a very ambitious undertaking”). Because of the relatively small collection, there’s not enough bottles of each to necessarily add them to their wine list, but these nightly pours allow patrons to sample their cellar while Rolo’s rebuilds.“Maybe it’ll be something we do indefinitely, or at least until we go through all these bottles,” says Bayless-Hall.

Whether it’s a Pierre Paillard Grand Cru Champagne or a Paolo Bea Italian red, Rolo’s loss is, at least temporarily, a wine lover’s gain. “I want people to be drinking wine that they’re excited about, and that I’m excited about, and that seems like something we’re going to be able to do in a way that’s kind of cool,” Bayless-Halls explains. “It’s for a shitty reason, but it’s ultimately exciting.”

title: A Bloody Mary for Every Mood
summary: Six takes on the brunch staple, from a nighttime version made with Scotch to a modern take with “celery air.”
content: A Bloody Mary is hard to ignore. Even the simplest ones are bright red and teeming with the punchiest ingredients in the pantry, while the garnishes of the most maximalist versions are fighting for space in the glass (and your attention). These days, it’s not just the brunch spots slinging them, it’s the chic lounges and the fancy science-driven bars serving their take, too. Here are some of our favorite ways to make the drink, for any occasion.

title: What It’s Like When Your Bar Is a Film Set
summary: Dante co-owner Linden Pride shares his experience—and the unforeseen challenges—of being featured on And Just Like That... and One Night Only.
content:
A certain apron caught my eye in the trailer for One Night Only. A bartender slides two shots over to Monica Barbaro’s and King Princess’ characters, donning the signature uniform of Dante, the aperitivo bar and restaurant that’s home to an iconic Garibaldi and a Punch-favorite Negroni. This, co-owner Linden Pride tells me, is not Dante’s first film rodeo. “We’ve used each of our restaurants in New York—Caffe Dante, Dante West Village, and Dante Aperitivo—as film sets,” he says, “and all of our experiences have been so different.”

I chatted with Pride about the ins and outs, costs, and challenges of having your space act as a film set.

title: This White Russian Got a Modern Makeover
summary: At Tavern Next Door, the disco-era drink has transformed into an Old-Fashioned that tastes like a malted milkshake.
content:
In Brooklyn, Red Hook Tavern’s much-buzzed-about dry-aged burger regularly draws dozens of hopeful diners into a queue that snakes down the block. Those in the know will tell you that you can now order the famous burger at Tavern Next Door, the new neighboring cocktail bar run by the same team. But Tavern Next Door, which is lit with a slight neon glow that evokes an Art Deco, midcentury supper club, is an experience in its own right. There, it’s head bartender Conor Johns’ inventive, ’70s-era disco drinks that take center stage. 

On the menu, under the banners of “Strong & Stiff” and “Shaken & Refreshing” are throwbacks like the Singapore Sling and Tequila Sunrise along with the Rusty Nail and Brandy Alexander. Johns uses the original names and many of the core components of each drink as familiar signposts, but employs unexpected ingredients and techniques that would be foreign to a bartender who pulled shifts at Studio 54 back in the day. 

That many of these oft-dismissed drinks are no longer ordered by cocktail enthusiasts is what makes them so special to Johns. “Keeping the original names helps put guests at ease and not feel intimidated by the modern twists, techniques and ingredients we’re incorporating,” he says. “The best compliments we get are that these drinks remind people of their past but in a new way to experience them.” 

Over several visits I’ve had the chance to sample my way through all of the drinks, but the one I can’t stop thinking about is the White Russian. I wondered whether you could really call a cocktail a White Russian if it wasn’t made with vodka and Kahlúa, but after trying it, it instantly won me over.

title: Break These Cocktail Rules
summary: Simple syrup in a Martini?!
content:
Last week, Amy Cavanaugh sung the praises of the Grilled Martini, a very summery take on the strong-and-stirred classic. Perhaps controversially, it’s served on the rocks. Popular in the ’50s (and gaining steam more recently), that presentation has its detractors, but my personal take? There’s a time and place for everything.

The Martini-on-the-rocks bravely breaks the rules (or at least turns some heads). So we thought it was a good time to revisit some other nonconforming cocktails whose creators—all trailblazing bartenders—had to break a rule or two to develop. Here are three ways that you, too, can go off the beaten path:

Traditional bartending wisdom would have you shake, not stir, drinks with juice. But drinks expert Al Sotack wanted to push back on that. For his South Bronx, a riff on the Bronx cocktail, he adds a tiny bit of pineapple and orange juices to make something close to a Martini with just a hint of citrus. His Algonquin, meanwhile, reads like a Manhattan. “A little tiny bit of juice doesn’t change the elegance,” he says.

(No, really!) It sounds like sacrilege, but “sugar is not the enemy,” says bar legend Joaquín Simó. With a light hand, a touch of sugar can add balance to drinks and bolster those that feel too much like “watery booze.” It certainly doesn’t work in every cocktail, and it should be used sparingly, but it’s worth a shot if you’re R&Ding and feel like your drink is too flabby or astringent.

The ingredients list for the Trinidad Sour does not contain a typo; it really does call for 1 1/2 ounces of Angostura bitters. The drink achieved modern classic-status for the shocking, flavor-packed move, and, like the similarly constructed Angostura Colada, has become an industry favorite. In bar settings, these cocktails are often prohibitively expensive, but if you’re looking for a one-of-a-kind at-home drink, put these recipes on your bucket list.

title: Nothing Says Summer Like a Grilled Martini
summary: Smoky brine and grilled Castelvetranos turn the strong-and-stirred drink into a warm-weather favorite.
content:
I’m a devoted Martini drinker, but long stretches of 95-degree days this summer had me rethinking my cocktail order. Unless a Martini comes with an icy sidecar (and the AC is blasting), the cocktail gets too warm, too fast. And drinking a strong, boozy cocktail when it’s that hot? Not the best idea.

Then I walked into Kansas City’s Varsity Club, a neighborhood basement bar with a ’70s feel, where I spied the Grilled Martini on the menu. Made with gin, dry vermouth and smoked olive brine, it’s garnished with a grilled olive. It sounded like the perfect summer Martini, something I could envision serving at a backyard cookout. Plus, to keep things cool, it’s served on the rocks.

When Caleb Roye, who owns the bar with his brother, Levi, opened Varsity Club, he “wanted to reconfigure classic cocktails and present them in an approachable way,” he says.

For their dirty Martini variation, the brothers tapped Turkish grilled olives, which they use to infuse a gin blend and garnish the drink. After attempting to grill olives themselves (“you have to borderline dehydrate olives before you grill them or else they just blister, and then you have to rehydrate them through marinating them,” says Roye of the complex process), they discovered grilled Castelvetrano olives from the brand Fora (you can buy them online). Grilled with char marks, the olives had the ideal meaty texture and natural smoky flavor they were seeking.

The base of the cocktail is a 50-50 blend of Citadelle Gin, which adds floral citrus notes to the drink, and Prairie Wolf Dry Gin, which provides structure and balance. To impart that savory grilled flavor, they sous vide the gin blend with olives and smoke olive brine with hickory. At the bar, they batch the gin and brine with dry vermouth and store it in the refrigerator, then shake and pour Martinis over ice for service. 

While true opponents of Martinis on the rocks can request the drink served up in a coupe, for Roye, the presentation is a key component. “I think serving a Martini on rocks makes it more approachable,” he says. The bar shakes the drink just briefly to “minimize dilution before it hits the glass and slowly dilutes in the guest’s hand.” And that makes it just the right drink to linger with over a lazy summer afternoon.

title: Five Underrated Tropical Classics
summary: From a little-known Daiquiri variation to the Philippines’ answer to a Singapore Sling and more.
content:
Between tiki-style drinks, the Caribbean classics and much more, tropical drinking is far from one thing. And hidden beneath the spotlight that favorites like the Mai Tai and the Piña Colada demand this time of year is a trove of lesser-known recipes that deserve more attention. These five cocktails—from a little-known Daiquiri variation to the Philippines’ answer to a Singapore Sling—are a good place to start.

The Pago Pago, essentially a Daiquiri made with Chartreuse and crème de cacao, was created by the rum brand Ronrico in the 1940s, and it appears in the second edition of Hyman Gale and Gerald F. Marco’s The How and When. While it’s not a tiki drink, the cocktail—which shares a name with the capital of Samoa—has some of the hallmarks of the genre. Paul McGee, who has revived the drink at Echo Lake, likens it to Donn the Beachcomber’s style.  “He’s best known for using dual citrus and layering a lot of different flavors,” McGee says. The cocktail has become a favorite among both rum nerds and those new to the spirit. “That’s the genius of this drink,” he says. “It’s so approachable, yet, if you look for it, you find the layers.”

title: There’s Benefits, And Then There’s These Benefits
summary: Offering everything from recipe “royalties” to spa services, some bars and restaurants are offering more than your average perks.
content:
“When I was working my way through the industry in my 20s and 30s, I was very rarely offered healthcare,” says Andrew Watts, proprietor of Cordelia and Rosy (which the restaurant styles as rosy) in Cleveland. “If healthcare was offered at all, it was only for management, carriers changed every year, it was hard to navigate, and it seemed very much an afterthought of something they had to do, not wanted to do. I had to beg for it far too often.” 

Watts is not alone. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, just 36 percent of service workers in the U.S. have access to employer-sponsored healthcare. Now, at his restaurant, Watts has prioritized “providing inclusive, all-encompassing care,” including by offering physical and mental health insurance to staff, hosting annual healthcare education sessions and partnering with local businesses on everything from spa visits to tattoo days (more on that in a bit!). 

In an industry where even basic benefits are hard to come by, there are a handful of bars, restaurants, and cafes that have taken a thoughtful approach to taking care of their staff, in turn attracting and retaining workers along the way. “You can’t pour out of an empty cup,” says Watts. “How can [hospitality workers] take care of others if they aren’t taken care of? This seems like such basic hospitality to me, yet few adhere to it.”

This week in Pre Shift, we’re bringing you some of those out-of-the-box ideas, from innovative pay structures to staff travel opportunities to local discounts. If you’re an operator looking for more ways to support your staff—or a staffer looking to advocate for your team—read on for those ideas, plus an update from last week’s newsletter and a handful of the hottest hospitality jobs right now.

Royalties, but for cocktails. Bar Bambi in Chicago has a unique approach to recipe crediting—something we’ve covered in this newsletter in the past. Bartenders who create cocktails that make it onto the Bar Bambi menu get a quarterly bonus based on sales of those drinks. “Basically, royalties for your creative work,” explains owner Katie Renshaw. 

Benefits that also benefit local businesses. Every month, the team behind Cesarina and Elvira in San Diego picks a nearby independent restaurant and opens a tab for staff to enjoy a meal. Also, once a week, employees can attend a complimentary yoga class across the street from Cesarina as a convenient way to recharge.

An exchange program. The restaurant Smoke Door has two locations: one in Lake Tahoe, California, and another in Yokohama, Japan. Owners Ryu Amemiya and Tyler Burges regularly send U.S. kitchen staff to stage at the Japanese location so they can learn more about Japanese flavors, techniques, and ingredients.

Covering the bases. Mark Okuda, chef-owner of LA’s The Brothers Sushi, gets his team tickets to watch the Dodgers on Japanese Heritage Night. Because the stadium allows fans to bring their own food, the staff brings homemade meals and hangs out for the night.

An underrated healthcare benefit. The New York nightclub Mansions offers its staff custom ear plugs.

An opportunity to level-up. Ayu Bakehouse in New Orleans created “Ayu Schoolhouse,” a paid educational program for employees that offers business (for example, a “How to Open a Food Pop-Up” series) and culinary (“The Science of Bread”) classes.

The dining room at Rosy.

A team break. Twice a year, Birdie’s in Austin closes for a two-week period. Staff can take the time to rest and recharge, and they’re paid for the full four weeks. 

The team that forages together, stays together. At Bosq in Aspen, chef Barclay Dodge leads the team on an annual research trip to different food destinations to explore local markets and forage. The trips are a chance for team-building, but they have also provided inspiration for R&D on Bosq’s menu.

An on-theme perk. The Museum Bar + Gift Shop, a recently opened NYC bar modeled after a natural history museum, plans to bring its staff on educational field trips (fittingly, to local museums).

Is there an award for best benefits? When Vinnie Cimino, chef at Cordelia, was nominated for a James Beard Award in 2024, Watts purchased tickets (which are hundreds of dollars) for any manager or sous chef who wanted to come celebrate. “We set up hosted events by doing collabs at a couple spots that made great spaces for our team to gather and celebrate with us,” says Watts. This year, 30 members of the team attended the ceremony, while more than 30 supported outside the theater in Chicago.

Cordelia and Rosy have also secured discounted spa services for staff by trading discounted meals with a local wellness studio and hosted free tattoo days with local artists. “I’ll always ask friends and fellow businesses to see how we can help each other,” says Watts. “We host collaborative events on the regular, as it’s central to our mission to give others a platform and attention.”

This is an excerpt from Pre Shift, our newsletter for bartenders, restaurant workers and the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more perspectives like this in your inbox.

title: The Most Popular Cocktails of July
summary: Here are the drinks that you couldn’t get enough of this month.
content: This month, the most popular recipes on Punch either took a page from the history books—whether that’s 1944’s Cocktail Guide and Ladies’ Companion, or 2007’s Imbibe! From Absinthe Cocktail to Whiskey Smash—or had a decidedly modern tack, using science and culinary techniques to transform highballs and aperitifs into high art. Here are the recipes you deemed best in July.

title: The ’Tinis, All Grown Up
summary: From an Appletini made with green Chartreuse and Suze to a frozen Pornstar Martini, here are six retro cocktails, revamped for the modern drinker.
content:
Ever since the Espresso Martini staged a dramatic return to the limelight a few years ago, the drink has remained a fixture of modern menus. It was the Trojan horse that paved the way for other caffeinated cocktails to make a splash, and it also emboldened the revival (and modernization) of its ’tini siblings. While these kitschy, crowd-pleasing drinks spent several years relegated to Dark-Age-drinks-status, now, thanks to nostalgia and a few modern tweaks, you can have an Appletini at a buzzy new bar and hardly anyone would bat an eye. Here is a look at the ’tinis you know and love, all all grown up.

According to Dale DeGroff, godfather of the modern cocktail revival, the French Martini was “one of the sparks that got the cocktail-as-Martini craze started.” A fruit-forward combination of vodka, pineapple juice and Chambord, the French Martini dates back to 1996 when DeGroff himself debuted the drink at restaurateur Keith McNally’s Pravda, in New York City. It wasn’t until the following year, however, when it hit the menu at McNally’s buzzy Balthazar, that the drink really took off. Though it may be less viral than its siblings, the French Martini, too, is making a comeback.

Traditional bartending wisdom would have you shake, not stir, drinks with juice. But drinks expert Al Sotack wanted to push back on that. For his South Bronx, a riff on the Bronx cocktail, he adds a tiny bit of pineapple and orange juices to make something close to a Martini with just a hint of citrus. His Algonquin, meanwhile, reads like a Manhattan. “A little tiny bit of juice doesn’t change the elegance,” he says.

(No, really!) It sounds like sacrilege, but “sugar is not the enemy,” says bar legend Joaquín Simó. With a light hand, a touch of sugar can add balance to drinks and bolster those that feel too much like “watery booze.” It certainly doesn’t work in every cocktail, and it should be used sparingly, but it’s worth a shot if you’re R&Ding and feel like your drink is too flabby or astringent.

The ingredients list for the Trinidad Sour does not contain a typo; it really does call for 1 1/2 ounces of Angostura bitters. The drink achieved modern classic-status for the shocking, flavor-packed move, and, like the similarly constructed Angostura Colada, has become an industry favorite. In bar settings, these cocktails are often prohibitively expensive, but if you’re looking for a one-of-a-kind at-home drink, put these recipes on your bucket list.

title: Nothing Says Summer Like a Grilled Martini
summary: Smoky brine and grilled Castelvetranos turn the strong-and-stirred drink into a warm-weather favorite.
content:
I’m a devoted Martini drinker, but long stretches of 95-degree days this summer had me rethinking my cocktail order. Unless a Martini comes with an icy sidecar (and the AC is blasting), the cocktail gets too warm, too fast. And drinking a strong, boozy cocktail when it’s that hot? Not the best idea.

Then I walked into Kansas City’s Varsity Club, a neighborhood basement bar with a ’70s feel, where I spied the Grilled Martini on the menu. Made with gin, dry vermouth and smoked olive brine, it’s garnished with a grilled olive. It sounded like the perfect summer Martini, something I could envision serving at a backyard cookout. Plus, to keep things cool, it’s served on the rocks.

When Caleb Roye, who owns the bar with his brother, Levi, opened Varsity Club, he “wanted to reconfigure classic cocktails and present them in an approachable way,” he says.

For their dirty Martini variation, the brothers tapped Turkish grilled olives, which they use to infuse a gin blend and garnish the drink. After attempting to grill olives themselves (“you have to borderline dehydrate olives before you grill them or else they just blister, and then you have to rehydrate them through marinating them,” says Roye of the complex process), they discovered grilled Castelvetrano olives from the brand Fora (you can buy them online). Grilled with char marks, the olives had the ideal meaty texture and natural smoky flavor they were seeking.

The base of the cocktail is a 50-50 blend of Citadelle Gin, which adds floral citrus notes to the drink, and Prairie Wolf Dry Gin, which provides structure and balance. To impart that savory grilled flavor, they sous vide the gin blend with olives and smoke olive brine with hickory. At the bar, they batch the gin and brine with dry vermouth and store it in the refrigerator, then shake and pour Martinis over ice for service. 

While true opponents of Martinis on the rocks can request the drink served up in a coupe, for Roye, the presentation is a key component. “I think serving a Martini on rocks makes it more approachable,” he says. The bar shakes the drink just briefly to “minimize dilution before it hits the glass and slowly dilutes in the guest’s hand.” And that makes it just the right drink to linger with over a lazy summer afternoon.

title: Five Underrated Tropical Classics
summary: From a little-known Daiquiri variation to the Philippines’ answer to a Singapore Sling and more.
content:
Between tiki-style drinks, the Caribbean classics and much more, tropical drinking is far from one thing. And hidden beneath the spotlight that favorites like the Mai Tai and the Piña Colada demand this time of year is a trove of lesser-known recipes that deserve more attention. These five cocktails—from a little-known Daiquiri variation to the Philippines’ answer to a Singapore Sling—are a good place to start.

The Pago Pago, essentially a Daiquiri made with Chartreuse and crème de cacao, was created by the rum brand Ronrico in the 1940s, and it appears in the second edition of Hyman Gale and Gerald F. Marco’s The How and When. While it’s not a tiki drink, the cocktail—which shares a name with the capital of Samoa—has some of the hallmarks of the genre. Paul McGee, who has revived the drink at Echo Lake, likens it to Donn the Beachcomber’s style.  “He’s best known for using dual citrus and layering a lot of different flavors,” McGee says. The cocktail has become a favorite among both rum nerds and those new to the spirit. “That’s the genius of this drink,” he says. “It’s so approachable, yet, if you look for it, you find the layers.”

title: There’s Benefits, And Then There’s These Benefits
summary: Offering everything from recipe “royalties” to spa services, some bars and restaurants are offering more than your average perks.
content:
“When I was working my way through the industry in my 20s and 30s, I was very rarely offered healthcare,” says Andrew Watts, proprietor of Cordelia and Rosy (which the restaurant styles as rosy) in Cleveland. “If healthcare was offered at all, it was only for management, carriers changed every year, it was hard to navigate, and it seemed very much an afterthought of something they had to do, not wanted to do. I had to beg for it far too often.” 

Watts is not alone. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, just 36 percent of service workers in the U.S. have access to employer-sponsored healthcare. Now, at his restaurant, Watts has prioritized “providing inclusive, all-encompassing care,” including by offering physical and mental health insurance to staff, hosting annual healthcare education sessions and partnering with local businesses on everything from spa visits to tattoo days (more on that in a bit!). 

In an industry where even basic benefits are hard to come by, there are a handful of bars, restaurants, and cafes that have taken a thoughtful approach to taking care of their staff, in turn attracting and retaining workers along the way. “You can’t pour out of an empty cup,” says Watts. “How can [hospitality workers] take care of others if they aren’t taken care of? This seems like such basic hospitality to me, yet few adhere to it.”

This week in Pre Shift, we’re bringing you some of those out-of-the-box ideas, from innovative pay structures to staff travel opportunities to local discounts. If you’re an operator looking for more ways to support your staff—or a staffer looking to advocate for your team—read on for those ideas, plus an update from last week’s newsletter and a handful of the hottest hospitality jobs right now.

Royalties, but for cocktails. Bar Bambi in Chicago has a unique approach to recipe crediting—something we’ve covered in this newsletter in the past. Bartenders who create cocktails that make it onto the Bar Bambi menu get a quarterly bonus based on sales of those drinks. “Basically, royalties for your creative work,” explains owner Katie Renshaw. 

Benefits that also benefit local businesses. Every month, the team behind Cesarina and Elvira in San Diego picks a nearby independent restaurant and opens a tab for staff to enjoy a meal. Also, once a week, employees can attend a complimentary yoga class across the street from Cesarina as a convenient way to recharge.

An exchange program. The restaurant Smoke Door has two locations: one in Lake Tahoe, California, and another in Yokohama, Japan. Owners Ryu Amemiya and Tyler Burges regularly send U.S. kitchen staff to stage at the Japanese location so they can learn more about Japanese flavors, techniques, and ingredients.

Covering the bases. Mark Okuda, chef-owner of LA’s The Brothers Sushi, gets his team tickets to watch the Dodgers on Japanese Heritage Night. Because the stadium allows fans to bring their own food, the staff brings homemade meals and hangs out for the night.

An underrated healthcare benefit. The New York nightclub Mansions offers its staff custom ear plugs.

An opportunity to level-up. Ayu Bakehouse in New Orleans created “Ayu Schoolhouse,” a paid educational program for employees that offers business (for example, a “How to Open a Food Pop-Up” series) and culinary (“The Science of Bread”) classes.

The dining room at Rosy.

A team break. Twice a year, Birdie’s in Austin closes for a two-week period. Staff can take the time to rest and recharge, and they’re paid for the full four weeks. 

The team that forages together, stays together. At Bosq in Aspen, chef Barclay Dodge leads the team on an annual research trip to different food destinations to explore local markets and forage. The trips are a chance for team-building, but they have also provided inspiration for R&D on Bosq’s menu.

An on-theme perk. The Museum Bar + Gift Shop, a recently opened NYC bar modeled after a natural history museum, plans to bring its staff on educational field trips (fittingly, to local museums).

Is there an award for best benefits? When Vinnie Cimino, chef at Cordelia, was nominated for a James Beard Award in 2024, Watts purchased tickets (which are hundreds of dollars) for any manager or sous chef who wanted to come celebrate. “We set up hosted events by doing collabs at a couple spots that made great spaces for our team to gather and celebrate with us,” says Watts. This year, 30 members of the team attended the ceremony, while more than 30 supported outside the theater in Chicago.

Cordelia and Rosy have also secured discounted spa services for staff by trading discounted meals with a local wellness studio and hosted free tattoo days with local artists. “I’ll always ask friends and fellow businesses to see how we can help each other,” says Watts. “We host collaborative events on the regular, as it’s central to our mission to give others a platform and attention.”
